passage:
"Sarita, can you water the tulsi and fold the towels before dinner?"
"Yes, Mummy! Of course!"
An hour later: "Sarita, the towels?"
"Oh! I forgot. Sorry! I'll do it right now!"
Half an hour later Himani-didi came in. "Mummy, the towels are still in the basket. And the tulsi's dry again."
"Sarita?"
"I totally forgot! My brain is so bad."
"That's the fifth time this week, beta."
Sarita looked at her toes. Didi sat down next to her. "You know what I think? I think you hate folding towels."
"...I do hate folding towels. They're so boring. And Didi only has to do the dishes."
"Then say that," Mummy said. "We can talk about swapping. But saying yes and then forgetting isn't fair on anyone."

qa.q: What two jobs did Mummy ask Sarita to do?
qa.a: Water the tulsi and fold the towels.

qa.q: Why did Sarita keep saying yes and then forgetting?
qa.a: Sarita felt resentful about the boring job, which seemed unfair next to Didi's dishes, but found it hard to say no directly, so the resistance came out as forgetting.

qa.q: Which choice in the conversation opened a better way forward?
qa.a: Didi naming the likely feeling, then Mummy inviting Sarita to say it and offering to talk about swapping. 🙂

qa.q: How might Himani-didi feel about the dry tulsi and the unfolded towels?
qa.a: Probably irritated at noticing the undone jobs again, and perhaps a little defensive when the dishes were brought up.

grounding: A child cheerfully agrees to a chore and keeps forgetting, until Mummy and Didi help Sarita say directly what the problem is.

passage:
Last month Rafiq Chacha from next door asked if I'd feed his parrots every evening while his leg was in plaster. I said, "Yes, yes, definitely!" And then, three evenings out of five, I "forgot". Mummy had to go instead, and she looked at me funny at dinner.
The truth, which I didn't even tell myself then, was that the parrots scare me. They screech and bite the bars when you open the cage. But Chacha is so kind, always giving me toffees, that saying no felt rude.
Last week Mummy asked why I kept agreeing. I cried a bit and told her. Then I told Chacha. He laughed and said, "Arre, just say so!" Now I water his plants instead. I'm Jahnavi, and plants don't bite.

qa.q: What did Rafiq Chacha ask Jahnavi to do?
qa.a: Feed his parrots every evening while his leg was in plaster.

qa.q: Why did Jahnavi keep 'forgetting' instead of saying no?
qa.a: Jahnavi was scared of the parrots but felt that saying no to kind Chacha would be rude, so the resistance came out sideways as forgetting.

qa.q: What turning point let Jahnavi stop forgetting?
qa.a: Telling Mummy the truth when she asked, then telling Chacha, which led to a new job Jahnavi could really do.

qa.q: How might Mummy have felt going to feed the parrots herself?
qa.a: Probably puzzled and a bit annoyed, sensing something was off, which is why she later asked Jahnavi why she kept agreeing.

grounding: A child who couldn't say no to a kind neighbour agreed to a frightening job and kept 'forgetting' it, until the truth came out.

passage:
Class 4 teacher's note, Friday
For three weeks Shreya has been on the rota to wipe the board and water the class plants. Each morning she agrees brightly, "Yes, Nazia Ma'am!", and each afternoon the board is still full and the plants are dry. When I remind her, she says, "Oh no, I totally forgot!" with a big smile.
Today I asked her quietly, "Is there a job on the rota you'd rather not do?" After a pause she said, "The chalk dust makes me sneeze, and the boys at the back laugh when I sneeze."
We've swapped her to handing out notebooks. I also told her she can always tell me no, or ask to swap, and I won't be cross.

qa.q: Which two jobs was Shreya on the rota for?
qa.a: Wiping the board and watering the class plants.

qa.q: Why might Shreya say 'I totally forgot!' with a big smile?
qa.a: She didn't want the board job because of the sneezing and the laughter, but felt she couldn't say no, so a cheerful 'forgot' was easier.

qa.q: Which choice of the teacher's worked, and why?
qa.a: Asking quietly whether there was a job Shreya would rather not do, and promising she could say no or swap, which made a direct refusal safe.

qa.q: What would change for Shreya now that Nazia Ma'am has said 'I won't be cross'?
qa.a: She may feel safe to say no openly next time, so she won't need to 'forget' to show she doesn't want a job.

grounding: A teacher notices a girl who agrees brightly to class jobs and then forgets them, and makes it safe for her to say no directly.

passage:
Dear Diary,
Today Ammi asked again if I'd go up and help Maria with her reading at six. I said, "Yes, Ammi, of course!" in my best voice. Then at six I suddenly had to sort my stickers. And have a long bath. By the time I came out it was seven, and Maria's mother had gone back upstairs.
That's the fourth time this week. Ammi thinks I'm just forgetful.
Truth is, I don't want to. Maria is six and she cries when she gets a word wrong, and it takes up all my cartoon time. But when Ammi asks, her face is so hopeful that "no" gets stuck. So "yes" comes out, and then my feet just go somewhere else.
Maybe tomorrow I'll forget again.
Dilnaz

qa.q: What did Dilnaz do at six instead of helping Maria?
qa.a: Sorted stickers and had a long bath.

qa.q: Why does "no" get stuck for Dilnaz?
qa.a: Ammi's face looks so hopeful that refusing feels impossible, so Dilnaz agrees cheerfully and then resists by "forgetting".

qa.q: What could Dilnaz try instead of forgetting again?
qa.a: Telling Ammi honestly that the sessions are hard and take all the cartoon time, and maybe offering two evenings a week instead of every day.

qa.q: What might Maria's mother think after going back upstairs four times?
qa.a: She may feel let down and puzzled, thinking Dilnaz is unreliable, without knowing Dilnaz never really wanted to say yes.

grounding: Shows a child who cheerfully agrees to an unwanted job and then keeps forgetting, because saying no directly feels impossible.

passage:
In their village near Thrissur, Umma and Elizabeth aunty from next door ran a small tea shop by the bus stop. Every afternoon Umma asked, "Salma, wash the glasses after school, okay?" and Salma, nine, said, "Yes, Umma! Of course!" with a big smile.
Every afternoon she then forgot. She went to see the ducks on the canal, or started a very long game of hopscotch. When she came back, the glasses were already shining on the rack.
On Friday Elizabeth aunty caught her arm, gently. "Salma, you say yes every day. And every day you disappear. Is there something about the glasses?"
Salma twisted her plait. "The soap smells horrible. It stays on my hands all evening. But Umma is so tired, I can't say no."
Elizabeth aunty laughed softly. "Then say that. We'll find you another job."

qa.q: Where did Salma go instead of washing the glasses?
qa.a: To see the ducks on the canal, or to start a very long game of hopscotch.

qa.q: Why did Salma keep saying "Yes, Umma!" if she didn't want to wash the glasses?
qa.a: Umma looked so tired that saying no felt wrong, so Salma agreed cheerfully and then resisted by disappearing instead.

qa.q: What did Elizabeth aunty's question make possible?
qa.a: It gave Salma a safe chance to say the real reason, the soap smell, so the job can be swapped instead of the forgetting going on 🙂

qa.q: How might Umma see the shining glasses on the rack each day?
qa.a: Umma may think Salma simply forgets, and perhaps feel tired or let down, not knowing Salma hates the soap but can't say so.

grounding: Illustrates a child who says yes brightly to a chore and then always slips away, her resistance coming out sideways because a direct no feels impossible.

Wednesday: "Mahima, Biscuit's dinner?" "Yes, of course!" At bedtime the bowl was still empty. "Sorry, sorry, I forgot again."
Friday: Maria aunty found the cat food tin hidden behind the flour. She sat down with Mahima. "You always say yes so happily. But you keep forgetting. Is there something about feeding Biscuit you don't like?" Mahima looked at her socks. "The food smells yucky. And he scratched me once." "Ah. You could have told me." Mahima shrugged. "You looked like you wanted a yes."

passage: Mridul, your amma says you keep "forgetting" to water the plants? Let your Jeevan thatha tell you a story. When I was nine, in Madurai, my job was to fetch milk from the dairy every morning at six. Every night my amma asked, "Jeevan, milk tomorrow?" and I said, "Yes, Amma!" with a big smile. And every morning, I forgot. I overslept, or lost the can. The truth was, there was a big black dog on the dairy road, and I was terrified of it. But I was too ashamed to say so. So I said yes and then didn't go. One day my grandfather asked me quietly, "Is it the milk you don't like, or the road?" I cried and told him about the dog. After that, he walked with me. And I never forgot again.

qa.q: What time was young Jeevan supposed to fetch the milk?
qa.a: At six.

qa.q: Why did young Jeevan say yes and then keep forgetting?
qa.a: He was terrified of the black dog and too ashamed to admit it, so he couldn't say no directly and his resistance came out as forgetting.

qa.q: What was the turning point in the story, and why did it work?
qa.a: His grandfather asking gently whether it was the milk or the road, which made it safe for Jeevan to tell the real reason.

qa.q: How might Jeevan's amma have felt each time the milk didn't come?
qa.a: His amma probably felt frustrated and angry, not knowing her son was scared.

grounding: Illustrates, through an elder's memory, a child saying yes cheerfully to a chore and forgetting each time because he couldn't say no directly.

passage: Exam week in their Chennai flat, and the water tanker came at unpredictable hours. "Kamal, when the tanker comes, fill the drums, okay?" Amma said. "Yes, Amma!" said Kamal, smiling. The tanker came at four. Kamal was reading comics on the terrace. The drums stayed empty. "Oh! I forgot!" Next day: "Yes, Amma, definitely!" The tanker came at seven. Kamal had his headphones on. Empty drums. On the third day, his sister Manjula filled them herself and then sat down next to him. "You always say yes, and then you always forget." Kamal went red. "The pipe is so heavy," he muttered. "And the tanker man shouts at me to hurry." "Then say that. Amma can't fix what she doesn't know." Kamal stared at his comic. "Every time I say no, she gets upset."

qa.q: At what time did the tanker come on the first day?
qa.a: At four.

qa.q: Why did Kamal keep smiling and saying yes if he didn't want to do it?
qa.a: He felt nervous about upsetting Amma by saying no, so his dislike of the heavy pipe and the shouting man came out as forgetting instead.

qa.q: What did Manjula suggest, and why would it help?
qa.a: Telling Amma the real reasons, so Amma could solve the problem instead of just being frustrated by empty drums.

qa.q: How might Manjula feel filling the drums herself?
qa.a: Manjula probably felt tired and a bit annoyed, but also curious about why her brother kept forgetting.

grounding: Shows a child cheerfully agreeing to fill water drums and then forgetting each time, the resistance coming out sideways instead of a direct no.

passage:
"Sumit, can you take the dustbin down to the gate before the van comes?" Kavitha called from the kitchen of their Hyderabad flat.

"Yes, Amma!" Sumit sang, cheerful as a bird, and kept building his cardboard robot.

The garbage van came and went. The bin stayed by the door.

It was the fourth time that week. Each time, the same bright "Yes!" and then nothing. On Tuesday he had forgotten to water the tulsi; on Thursday, to fold the clothes.

That evening Kavitha sat beside the robot. "You say yes very nicely. But maybe you don't want to do the bin at all?" Sumit's hands stopped. "It smells," he muttered. "And it's always me." Kavitha nodded. "Thank you for telling me. Let's make a list, and you can swap jobs with your sister sometimes."

qa.q: What was Sumit building when he said yes?
qa.a: Sumit was building his cardboard robot.

qa.q: Why might Sumit keep saying a cheerful "Yes!" and then forgetting?
qa.a: Sumit feels resentful that the bin is always his job but can't say no directly, so the resistance comes out as forgetting.

qa.q: What did Kavitha's question get right?
qa.a: She named the pattern gently and made it safe to say no, which let Sumit admit the real reasons so they could share the jobs.

qa.q: How might Kavitha feel after the fourth forgotten bin?
qa.a: Kavitha probably felt frustrated and puzzled at first, then curious enough to ask what was really going on.

grounding: Shows a boy who cheerfully agrees to chores and keeps forgetting, until his mother makes it safe to say what he resents.

passage:
"Dolma, you'll feed Momo before school, right?"
"Yes, yes, of course!"
Next morning Momo the cat was yowling at an empty bowl.
"Dolma! You said yes."
"Oh no, I totally forgot, Sahil dai! Sorry!" She smiled her sweetest smile.
"That's what you said on Monday. And Wednesday."
"I have a lot on my mind."
Sahil crouched by the bowl. "Can I ask something? Do you actually want to feed Momo?"
Dolma twisted her plait. "Not in the morning. I'm always late for the bus. And you never asked if I wanted to. You just said I would."
"Ah." Sahil scratched his head. "Okay. What if you do evenings and I do mornings?"
"Evenings," Dolma said. "Deal."
That evening Momo's bowl was full by six.

qa.q: Who is Momo?
qa.a: Momo is the cat.

qa.q: What might Dolma really feel about feeding Momo in the mornings?
qa.a: Dolma seems resentful, rushed and never asked, so instead of saying no she keeps cheerfully forgetting.

qa.q: What did Sahil do that ended the forgetting?
qa.a: He asked directly whether Dolma wanted the job, listened, and offered a swap, so she could say what she wanted openly.

qa.q: How might Sahil dai see the forgetting before he asks?
qa.a: Sahil probably felt irritated and let down, with Momo yowling at an empty bowl again.

grounding: Shows a girl who says yes to feeding the cat and keeps forgetting, until her brother asks what she really wants.

passage:
I'm Himani, and last year, when Kalyani Mausi came to live with us, she asked me to peel the potatoes every evening. I always said, "Yes, Mausi, sure!" with a big smile. Then I'd forget. I'd be in the bath. Or doing homework. Or I'd peel two potatoes and leave the rest.

It wasn't really forgetting. I didn't want to do it, because before Mausi came, evenings were my drawing time. But she was a guest, and I didn't know how to say no to a grown-up.

One evening she found me drawing and said, "Himani, if you don't want to peel, you can tell me." I burst into tears and said everything. She laughed and said, "Then draw me a picture instead, and peel only on Sundays." Now I peel on Sundays, properly, and she has my drawings on her wall.

qa.q: What did Kalyani Mausi ask Himani to do every evening?
qa.a: Mausi asked Himani to peel the potatoes every evening.

qa.q: Why did Himani keep forgetting the potatoes?
qa.a: Himani felt resentful about losing drawing time but was too nervous to say no to a grown-up guest, so the refusal came out as forgetting.

qa.q: Which choice worked, and why?
qa.a: Mausi made it safe to say no, and they agreed on Sundays, so the resistance could be said openly instead of sideways.

qa.q: How might Kalyani Mausi have felt about the half-peeled potatoes?
qa.a: Mausi may have felt puzzled and a little unwelcome at first, before understanding how much the drawing time mattered.

grounding: A child looks back on saying yes to a chore and then forgetting, because saying no to a grown-up felt impossible.

passage:
After-school club notes, Diwali week, by Gurleen (club supervisor).
Monday: Asked Abhinav to stack the chairs after craft time. He grinned, "Yes, sure!" Twenty minutes later he was at the diya-painting table, chairs untouched. He said, "Oh, I forgot."
Tuesday and Wednesday: Same cheerful yes, same forgetting. Each time he was painting diyas or stringing marigolds instead.
Thursday: I sat beside him while he painted and asked quietly, "Do you really forget, or do you not want to stack chairs?" He went pink. "The others get to finish their diyas. I always get chairs."
He was right; I had asked him four days running.
What I did next: made a rota on the board, with every child's name, and told Abhinav he could say "not now, after my diya" instead of saying yes. On Friday he said exactly that, and then stacked the chairs.

qa.q: What was Abhinav doing each time the chairs needed stacking?
qa.a: He was painting diyas or stringing marigolds instead.

qa.q: Why did Abhinav keep saying a cheerful yes and then forgetting?
qa.a: He felt it was unfair to always get the chairs, and saying no to an adult felt too hard, so his annoyance came out as forgetting.

qa.q: What did Gurleen change that helped Abhinav?
qa.a: Gurleen shared the job with a rota and gave Abhinav words to say "not now" honestly, so he no longer needed to forget.

qa.q: What would change if Gurleen had just scolded Abhinav for forgetting?
qa.a: Abhinav would likely keep saying yes and forgetting, and the real problem, always being picked, would stay hidden.

grounding: Illustrates a child who says yes cheerfully to a chore and forgets each time because he cannot say no directly, seen through a supervisor's festival-week notes.

passage:
Monsoon diary, Tuesday
It rained AGAIN today. Amma shouted from the kitchen, "Santosh, bring the clothes in from the terrace!" I said, "Yes Amma, coming!" and finished my comic. When I went up, everything was soaking. Amma sighed and said, "You forgot again?" I nodded.
But diary, I did not forget. I heard the thunder. I just did not want to go. Chetan never has to bring clothes in because he is "too small", but he is eight and he can carry socks. Every rainy day it is me, me, me.
I can't say that to Amma, because she is already tired from work, and she would say, "Don't argue." So I say yes and then I forget. It's like a secret no.
Tomorrow it will rain again. Maybe I will ask if Chetan can carry the socks at least.

qa.q: What was on the terrace when it rained?
qa.a: The clothes were on the terrace, and when Santosh went up everything was soaking.

qa.q: How does Santosh feel about bringing the clothes in, and why does Santosh pretend to forget?
qa.a: Santosh feels resentful that it is always their job and not Chetan's, but is scared of arguing with a tired Amma, so forgetting works as a secret no.

qa.q: What small step could Santosh try next time instead of forgetting?
qa.a: Santosh could tell Amma calmly that it feels unfair and ask if Chetan can carry the socks, so the job is shared out loud.

qa.q: How might Amma see the soaked clothes each rainy day?
qa.a: Amma probably feels tired and let down, thinking Santosh is careless, without knowing there is a real complaint behind the forgetting.

grounding: A child in the monsoon cheerfully agrees to a chore and then forgets on purpose, because saying a direct no feels impossible.

passage: On the first morning of Pongal in the village, Hansa Paati handed Deepika the broom. "Sweep the front yard before your cousins start the kolam, kanna." Deepika smiled wide. "Yes, Paati!" Then she skipped next door to see the calves with painted horns. The cousins, carrying rice flour, had to sweep the leaves themselves. The second morning, the same. On the third, Paati found the broom lying exactly where Deepika had leaned it. Paati waited on the step. When Deepika returned, Paati asked, "Kanna, you say yes so sweetly. Why does the yard never get swept?" Deepika twisted her skirt. "Because I sweep and they get to draw. I never get to draw." Paati nodded slowly. "Then tomorrow you sweep half, and you draw the middle."

qa.q: Where did Deepika go instead of sweeping the yard?
qa.a: She skipped next door to see the calves with painted horns.

qa.q: Why did Deepika keep saying yes and then leaving the yard unswept?
qa.a: She felt left out and jealous that her cousins got to draw the kolam while she only swept, but she could not say no to Paati directly.

qa.q: What did Paati do that helped the real problem come out?
qa.a: Paati sat and waited, then asked gently why the yard never got swept, and when she heard the reason she changed the jobs so Deepika could draw too.

qa.q: How might the cousins have seen Deepika's forgetting?
qa.a: The cousins may have felt annoyed at sweeping leaves every morning, thinking Deepika was lazy, not knowing she felt shut out of the kolam.

grounding: During Pongal a village girl agrees sweetly to sweep and forgets every morning, because she cannot say that she resents never drawing the kolam.

passage:
During the snowy week of the school holidays in Istanbul, Anne asked Elif every morning to shovel the front step and feed the cat. "Of course, Anne!" Elif sang each time, all smiles.
By noon the step was still white and the cat was yowling. Her older brother Siddiq ended up doing both. "I forgot!" Elif said on Monday, and Tuesday, and Wednesday, each time with a big innocent grin.
On Thursday Siddiq found her building a snowman right beside the unshovelled step. "You didn't forget," he said. "You just don't want to do it."
Elif's smile slipped. "The shovel is heavy and my fingers freeze," she muttered. "But Anne always looks so tired when she asks."

qa.q: Which two chores did Anne ask Elif to do?
qa.a: Shovel the front step and feed the cat.

qa.q: Why did Elif keep saying yes cheerfully and then forgetting?
qa.a: She did not want to do the cold, heavy chores but felt uneasy saying no to a tired Anne, so her reluctance came out as forgetting.

qa.q: What could help Elif and Anne?
qa.a: Elif could say honestly that the shovel is too heavy, and Anne could offer a swap, such as Elif feeding the cat while someone else shovels.

qa.q: How does Siddiq feel about Elif's forgetting?
qa.a: He is frustrated at doing both chores and sees through her "I forgot" to the real reluctance.

grounding: A child cheerfully agrees to chores and then keeps forgetting, because saying no directly feels impossible.
